I have been building software for close to 30 years, the last several at staff and principal level: Staff Engineer at ServiceTitan and Blankfactor, currently acting Principal Developer/Architect on a greenfield election management platform, with lead developer and architect roles before that. What those have in common is owning technical direction for a system and staying accountable for it long after the first release, usually on the pieces other engineers end up depending on. At ServiceTitan I led the design and did the principal development on the customer-facing API surface that external integrators build against, which means I have lived with the part people tend to skip: you cannot quietly rename a field, and someone is still calling the thing you shipped a year later. At Runbeck I designed a reusable authentication and role-based access control service used across the company's applications, with persistence behind a key/value interface so the same codebase ran embedded on ARM hardware supplied to customers, inside customer infrastructure, and in the cloud. Designing for consumers I could not see yet, and finding out later whether the abstraction held up, is the part of that work I learned the most from.

The rest of my background is broad by design. I have written JavaScript since 1997 and TypeScript since 2013, across Node services, GraphQL layers, React front ends and serverless work on Lambda and Cloudflare Workers, alongside twenty-five years of C# and .NET. I have worked with Kafka, RabbitMQ and cloud queues on production systems, built build tooling and code generation that other teams used daily, and spent enough time in databases to have opinions about where logic belongs. My current contract is mostly C# and .NET, though the front end is React and I wrote most of the build and automation tooling in TypeScript under Deno.

At this level most of the leverage is not in the code I write. It is in the standards that get set, the reviews I give, and whether the next engineer can pick the system up without me in the room. I write designs down before building them and record decisions along with the alternative that lost and why, which costs very little and saves a great deal two years later. I have established front-end practice and mentored developers on a team that needed both, sat on a platform architecture team, and spent a year arguing a large company toward a stack it had not adopted yet. I also read and experiment on my own time, something like fifteen hours a week and for most of my career, tracking a wide surface shallowly and going deep only where I actually need to. My main opinion about architecture is that the cost of an abstraction is paid by every team that has to use it, so it had better be earning its place.

On AI tooling, I use it daily, mostly on personal projects: reverse engineering and documenting an old platform for preservation, and a cross-runtime database adapter written in Rust. My working position is that agents are a throughput multiplier bounded by human review capacity rather than by spend, which makes documentation and tests the review surface rather than an afterthought. It is very good at reading code it has never seen, and wrong often enough that I check anything I would put my name on.

I would welcome the chance to talk about the work and where I would have the most leverage.
